newsitem.title: UK: UK "spark spread" trading to boom in next few year.
newsitem.headline: UK "spark spread" trading to boom in next few year.

text.p: Trading the price differential between gas and electricity in the UK is set to boom over the next few years but so far it has not become a reality, an electricity industry conference was told on Thursday.

"With the present tranche of gas powered generation, you can park the question of arbitrage between gas and electricity. It's not happening," said John Saunders, director of regulation and business affairs at electricity regulator Offer.

A generator operating a Combined Cycle Generating Turbine (CCGT), which allows the option of burning fuels other than gas to generate electricity, may find the electricity price falls below the gas price.

In this case, if the margin between the two is wide enough, the generator may choose to sell gas on the market instead of burning it, and either burning alternative fuels or temporarily withdrawing from generation.
Saunders added that for arbitrage, sometimes called the "spark spread", to function properly, electricity generators need "personal control" over gas supply.

But most generators take gas on "interruptible" contracts. Under this system suppliers have the option of cutting gas deliveries and diverting them elsewhere, usually for up to 45 days a year, in exchange for cheaper prices to generators. And generators are not usually offered gas supplies on a "firm" basis, where deliveries are guaranteed.

Duncan Sinclair, managing consultant of consultants Caminus Energy Ltd, agreed that arbitrage or spread trading has not yet become established. But he expects this to change as gas fired plants take over a larger share of total electricity generation.
"In 1990 there was virtually no gas plant in the UK," he said. "But by 2000 about half of all electricity will come from gas, consuming about a third of all gas used in the UK."

Sinclair said that last winter there was only one day on which gas prices exceeded electricity prices for long enough to make arbitrage workable. But both Sinclair and Neil Bryson, chairman of the Electricity Pool of England and Wales, agreed that the price relationship will change.

This is because gas prices have already fallen significantly since the market was deregulated and restructured. But electricity market restructuring still has some way to go, they said, and electricity prices are expected to fall significantly.
The next generation of power plant will be so-called Merchant Plants, Sinclair said.
These have a lower load factor than traditional plant, and higher flexibility. This flexibility allows them to switch between gas and other fuels more quickly than current plant.
This will allow them to take advantage of short-term price movements on the electricity market where prices are currently set by the pool on a half-hour by half-hour basis.

At present, he said, of 13 GigaWatts (GW) of CCGT capacity in the UK, around 4 GW could now be used for arbitraging. This is mainly from plant belonging to generators National Power, PowerGen and Eastern Group, as they have the most flexibility, he said.

But a further 6 GW of capacity is potentially subject to interruption. So a combination of physical constraints leading to interruption, and market circumstances leading to arbitrage opportunities, could already remove 10 GW of capacity from the system, out of a peak demand of approximately 50 GW.
"Even now a big chunk is vulnerable to being taken off," he said. "This will increase towards 2000."

Within a few years, Sinclair believes, a new group of dealers trading the gas to electricity arbitrage will be employed throughout the industry, probably trading power derivatives relating to both gas and electricity, and enhancing overall security of supply as well as reducing price volatility for consumers.
